newsitem.title: USA: Study finds estrogen-breast cancer link.
newsitem.headline: Study finds estrogen-breast cancer link.

text.p: Older women with the strongest bones tend to face the greatest risk of breast cancer and exposure to the female hormone oestrogen may play a key role, according to a study to be published on Thursday.
The findings reported in the New England Journal of Medicine are based on the Framingham Study, named after the Massachusetts town where residents have had their health tested extensively since 1948.

The conclusions may someday help doctors better predict which women face a higher risk of breast cancer. Those women can then try to catch the disease when it is most curable, in its earliest stages, using frequent breast X-rays.

The study led by Yuqing Zhang of the Boston University School of Medicine assessed the bone densities of 1,373 women and checked to see if they developed breast cancer. After menopause, breast tumours appeared in 91 women.

When they compared the likelihood of getting the cancer to the density of each woman's finger bones they found the breast cancer rate was 3.5 times greater among the 25 percent with the densest bones than for those with lowest bone densities.

The work suggests a link between breast cancer and oestrogen because the female hormone is known to keep bones strong and dense. But the researchers did not recommend that women give up oestrogen supplements.

Older women need the hormone to keep their bones from becoming brittle, a condition that can be life-threatening in itself. Oestrogen also protects against heart disease, which kills eight times as many women as breast cancer.

Dr. David Felson of Boston University, a co-author of the study, said "the link between high bone density and breast cancer may be due to other factors and that oestrogen use has other positive health effects" that may outweigh the risks.
"Although the biologic mechanisms linking bone mass to the risk for breast cancer are not fully understood," the Zhang team said, "cumulative exposure to oestrogen may have a role."
Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer among women in the United States, striking about 180,000 each year.

Dr. Joan McGowan of the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases said researchers "need to clarify if oestrogen is the link between bone mass and breast cancer, and if it is whether it is lifetime exposure or effects that occur at a critical period, such as adolescence."
